opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, working on hard theoretical problems is a lot like wandering in a dark room. You know there's something there, maybe a door or a way out, but most of the time you can't see anything. You try one direction, hit a wall, back up, and try another. Most days you feel like you're making no progress at all.

What people don't always realize is how much of the work is failure. You come up with an idea, spend a week or two developing it, and then find a counterexample that breaks the whole thing. You have to accept that this is normal. The skill isn't avoiding dead ends. It's learning something from each one, so that even a failed attempt narrows down where the answer might be.

There's also a lot of patience involved, and a kind of stubbornness. Sometimes you carry a problem around in your head for months. You think about it on walks or before you fall asleep. Then one day, often when you're not trying, two pieces you'd been holding separately suddenly connect. That moment, when everything clicks and you can see the whole structure clearly, is incredibly rewarding. It's rare, but it's what keeps you going through all the confusion.

I'd also say it's become less of a solitary activity than people imagine. Talking with collaborators, explaining your half-formed idea out loud, and having someone poke holes in it is often what moves things forward. So it's a mix of deep individual focus and good conversations.

Over time, I found that the habits from that kind of research carried over even when I moved toward more systems-oriented and practical work. You break a big, intimidating problem into precise smaller questions, you stay comfortable with not knowing for a long time, and you trust that rigor will eventually get you somewhere. That mindset has been really valuable to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes trying ideas, learning from failures, and thinking patiently, but does not say abstract thinking is essentially the only available way to work on these problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate says progress can feel absent and mentions thinking on walks or before sleep, but does not observe that the work can outwardly look like idleness.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd describe it as a lot of slow, patient wandering before anything clicks. When you start on a hard theoretical problem, you usually don't even know what the right question is yet. So much of the early work is just reading, re-deriving things by hand, and trying small cases until you build intuition for where the difficulty actually lives.

Most days feel unproductive in the moment. You try an approach, it fails, you try to understand exactly why it fails, and that failure mode often becomes the real insight. I've learned to treat dead ends as information rather than wasted time. The progress is rarely linear. You can be stuck for weeks, and then one reframing, sometimes from a completely different area, makes a whole chain of things fall into place.

The other part people underestimate is how collaborative and conversational it is. Explaining a half-formed idea to a colleague on a whiteboard forces you to make it precise, and that precision is where mistakes and opportunities show up. Beyond the mathematics, it's about taste. Knowing which problems are worth your time, and which simplifying assumptions you can make without losing the essence. That taste only comes from having been wrong many times, so I think persistence and a kind of comfort with confusion are the core skills.

r001.rationale: The response describes reading, re-deriving, and trying approaches, but does not say abstract thinking is essentially the only available way to work on these problems.

r002.rationale: It says most days feel unproductive in the moment, but does not describe the work as outwardly appearing idle.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe it as a process of turning something you don’t understand into a question you can work on. You start with an intuition, try a few simple cases, and see whether you can make that intuition precise. Often, when you try to prove it, you discover a gap—or a counterexample that forces you to rethink the question.

So a lot of the work is spent being stuck. You try an approach, figure out why it fails, and gradually understand the structure of the problem better. Progress doesn’t necessarily mean proving a theorem that day. Sometimes it means realizing which assumption matters, or why a seemingly promising path won’t work. Those small insights can eventually make the solution possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intuition, examples, proofs, and understanding structure, but does not say abstract thinking is essentially the only available way to tackle such problems.

r002.rationale: It says much of the work involves being stuck, but does not observe that this work can outwardly look like idleness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a process of turning something you don’t understand into smaller questions you can work on. You start with intuition, try simple examples, and see where your assumptions break. Often you spend a lot of time on an approach that doesn’t work, but that can still teach you something important about the problem.

The difficult part is that effort doesn’t translate into progress in a predictable way. You can be stuck for days, and then one observation changes how you see everything. So the work takes both rigor and creativity—and patience with uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response mentions intuition, examples, rigor, and creativity, but does not say that abstract thinking is essentially the only available way to work on these problems.

r002.rationale: It describes being stuck and making unpredictable progress, but does not observe that the work can outwardly look like idleness.
